title: Los Angeles breakup, the warehouse job, Noble Sissle, and Jeter-Pillars in St. Louis
summary: Harlan Leonard's band broke up in Los Angeles, Moore worked briefly in a warehouse, toured with Noble Sissle, and landed in St. Louis with Jeter-Pillars where Armstrong's men heard him.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Second try at it. How did that take place and when?
I left Kansas City with Harlan Leonard and we went straight to the West coast, to Los Angeles. In Los Angeles there was no place for the big bands at all now, and the band broke up.
This was during the war still.

What were some of the reasons for that, there being no place for big bands other than the fact that some of the clubs I guess weren't available and some of the dancing places people couldn't afford to have a band in, but were there any other reasons?

No, just that money was scarce then, everything was put in the war effort. You had to tighten your belt main reason they broke up the bands during that time, couldn't find a job playing music. So I looked for the employment pages in the newspapers and ended up being a warehouse man for an oil company. And we were hoisting 500, 600 pound oil drums pull them up by a pulley, and arranging the drums to the sail. Different intricacies of doing warehouse work. And I stayed there about two or three days until Noble Sissle came out to the Cotton Club and he was getting ready to

break the band up, I guess. So he wants to get out of Los Angeles. So he wanted an attraction. He heard of me and called me at my hotel, and said, "Come on. Would you like to go with me? I'm going up to British Columbia on a theater tour." I said, sure. So he said, "Quit your job. You don't belong in a warehouse." So four days I worked, and then finally I left to go with Noble Sissle, up in British Columbia, Seattle, Portland, San Francisco. And on the way back to the east, and finally once again, the band broke up in St. Louis.

And in St. Louis I got a job with Jeter-Pillars who played at the Jordan-Chambers Club, and Louie Armstrong was in St. Louis, they heard of me through the grapevine that I was capable of making good with them, I guess so they sent Teddy McRae and a bunch of musicians from the Armstrong band over to the club where I worked and I did my special number, I don't remember what specialty I did on the floor show, so they said, "We [you] want to join our band." "I'd be happy to." All right, we've heard of your reputation and attraction musically on the trombone, we'd like an we will send for you when we get to New York."
That's the way I got to New York.
